note: Observances and anniversaries are chosen by this site's editors. Each links to a page that confirms its date; movable holidays list the dates for 2026 to 2028 only.

items.m: Annual May heritage month honoring Asian American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander history and contributions; the main yearly peak for AAPI-focused content.
Congress recognized October as Filipino American History Month starting with a 2009 Senate resolution; FANHS has marked the month since 1991.
Community observance of the day in 1942 that Executive Order 9066 was signed, leading to the wartime removal and incarceration of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry.

items.t: Fred Korematsu Day of Civil Liberties and the Constitution
items.m: California's annual day honoring civil rights litigant Fred Korematsu, kept on his January 30 birthday; a hook for civil liberties and immigration-policy coverage.
Start of the lunar year, celebrated by Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese and other Asian American communities; a major annual hook for community, business and policy content.
Vietnamese lunar new year, the biggest family and community holiday for Vietnamese Americans, with festivals and temple and market events in the days around it.
Festival of lights marked by Hindu, Sikh, Jain and some Buddhist communities; dates shown are the main Lakshmi Puja day and can differ by a day by region.
Harvest-moon festival on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month, celebrated with mooncakes and family gatherings by Chinese, Vietnamese and other communities.
Korean harvest and ancestor-remembrance holiday on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month; dates shown are Chuseok day itself within a three-day Korean holiday.
Spring harvest festival and Punjabi and Sikh new-year observance marked with parades and community events; listed dates follow the solar-calendar sources.

items.t: Songkran and Southeast Asian New Year
items.m: Mid-April new year festivals in Thailand (Songkran), Laos (Pi Mai) and Cambodia (Khmer New Year), with temple and water-blessing events in diaspora communities.
items.o: Southeast Asian Ministers of Education Organization (SEAMEO)

items.m: Marks the January 13, 1903 arrival of the first Korean immigrants in Hawaii; recognized by House resolutions and state proclamations and a hook for Korean American history content.
Hawaii state holiday on March 26 honoring Prince Kuhio, a Hawaiian royal and delegate to Congress; a Native Hawaiian civic and policy content hook.
Hawaii state holiday on June 11 honoring Kamehameha I, who united the Hawaiian Islands; observed with parades, lei draping and cultural events.
Hawaii observance on May 1, set in state law as May Day is Lei Day, celebrating lei and Hawaiian culture; it falls on the first day of AAPI Heritage Month.
Hawaii state holiday on the third Friday of August marking admission as the 50th state; 2028 date is computed from the statutory third-Friday rule.
Legal public holiday in Guam on July 21 marking the 1944 liberation from Japanese occupation; a major CHamoru civic event and military-history hook.
Marks the April 17, 1900 Deed of Cession of Tutuila and Aunu'u to the United States; listed as a public holiday in American Samoa and marked by Samoan communities elsewhere.
March 1 observance in the Marshall Islands recalling people harmed by U.S. nuclear testing, anchored to the 1954 Castle Bravo test; ties to compensation and Compact debates.
April 17 marks the 1975 fall of Phnom Penh to the Khmer Rouge; recognized by several U.S. cities, counties and a state, and a hook for Cambodian American remembrance and refugee stories.
President Carter signed Public Law 95-419 (signing date) creating Asian/Pacific American Heritage Week for 1979, the origin of today's May heritage month.
items.o: U.S. Government Publishing Office (Statutes at Large)

items.t: Luzones Indios land at Morro Bay
items.m: Date cited by Congress and FANHS for the earliest documented Filipino presence in the continental U.S.; the historical anchor for Filipino American History Month.
First transcontinental railroad completed at Promontory Summit, Utah; Chinese laborers built much of the Central Pacific line, a standard Heritage Month hook.
President Grant signed the Page Act, which targeted the immigration of Chinese women and is a common reference point for the history of federal immigration restriction.
President Arthur signed the law suspending Chinese labor immigration; widely cited as the first major federal law to bar a group by national origin.
Supreme Court decision holding that a man born in San Francisco to Chinese parents was a U.S. citizen; a frequent reference in birthright citizenship coverage.
items.o: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School

items.m: The San Francisco Bay immigration station opened; it processed Asian and other immigrants and is central to the exclusion-era history of Chinese Americans.
Married Women's Independent Citizenship Act; it still stripped citizenship from American women who married men 'ineligible for citizenship,' chiefly Asian immigrants.
Supreme Court held that Bhagat Singh Thind, an Indian Sikh veteran, was not a 'white person' eligible for naturalization; a core South Asian American history hook.
items.o: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School

items.m: Signed by President Coolidge; set national-origins quotas and barred entry of those ineligible for citizenship, effectively ending most Asian immigration.
President Roosevelt signed the law setting a ten-year Commonwealth period leading to Philippine independence; a key moment in Filipino American immigration history.
President Roosevelt signed the order that led to the removal and incarceration of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry on the West Coast.
President Roosevelt signed the Magnuson Act repealing the Chinese Exclusion Acts, a milestone for Chinese immigrants' access to naturalization.
Supreme Court upheld, 6-3, Fred Korematsu's conviction for violating a wartime exclusion order; a central case in civil-liberties and Japanese American history.
items.o: Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts

items.m: Truman approved the act opening naturalization to people of races indigenous to India and the Philippines and setting small annual immigration quotas for each.
items.o: U.S. Government Publishing Office (Statutes at Large)

items.t: Philippine independence from the United States
items.m: The U.S. recognized Philippine independence and the two countries signed the Treaty of General Relations in Manila; a Filipino American history hook.
items.o: Office of the Historian, U.S. Department of State

items.t: Dalip Singh Saund takes House seat
items.m: Saund of California, elected in November 1956, was sworn in as the first Asian American and first Sikh elected to Congress.
Eisenhower proclaimed Hawaii a state on this date; he had signed the Admission Act on March 18, 1959. Hook for Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander history.
items.o: National Archives (Office of the Federal Register)

items.t: Hiram Fong seated in the U.S. Senate
items.m: Hiram Fong was seated as one of Hawaii's first two U.S. senators after statehood; he is widely recognized as the first Asian American senator.
Patsy Mink of Hawaii was sworn in as the first Asian American woman and first woman of color to serve in Congress.
President Johnson signed the law at the Statue of Liberty; it replaced national-origins quotas and led to major growth in Asian immigration.
Saigon fell, ending the Vietnam War and starting a refugee exodus; Vietnamese Americans mark the date as Black April, a remembrance and community-history hook.
items.o: Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training

items.t: Voting Rights Act language-minority amendments signed
items.m: President Ford signed amendments extending protections to language minorities, expressly including Asian Americans; the basis for multilingual ballots and assistance.
items.o: U.S. Government Publishing Office (Statutes at Large)

items.m: President Carter signed the law creating a standard system for admitting and resettling refugees; central to the history of Southeast Asian resettlement.
Chin died four days after being beaten in Highland Park, Michigan on June 19, 1982; his case galvanized Asian American civil rights organizing.
President Reagan signed the law apologizing for the wartime incarceration of Japanese Americans and authorizing redress payments to survivors.
The Rodney King trial verdict set off days of unrest in Los Angeles; Korean Americans call the date Sa-I-Gu (4-2-9), and Koreatown businesses were hard hit.
Queen Liliuokalani was deposed on this date; Native Hawaiian organizations mark the anniversary, and Congress cited it in the 1993 Apology Resolution.
Congress's joint resolution (Public Law 103-150), approved this date, apologized to Native Hawaiians for the 1893 overthrow of the Kingdom of Hawaii.
items.o: U.S. Government Publishing Office (Statutes at Large)

items.t: Palau Compact of Free Association takes effect
items.m: The Compact with Palau took effect on this date (proclaimed Sept. 27, 1994), ending the trusteeship; COFA migrants' access to U.S. services is an ongoing policy topic.
items.o: The American Presidency Project, UC Santa Barbara

items.t: Marshall Islands Compact of Free Association takes effect
items.m: The Compact with the Marshall Islands took full effect on this date; it frames U.S.-RMI relations, including Marshallese residency rights in the United States.
President Clinton signed the order creating the White House Initiative and President's Advisory Commission on Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders.
President Clinton signed Public Law 106-207, easing naturalization for certain Hmong and Lao veterans who served alongside U.S. forces in Laos.
Sikh business owner Balbir Singh Sodhi was shot outside his Mesa, Arizona gas station days after 9/11, widely cited as the first post-9/11 hate-crime murder.
items.o: Sikh American Legal Defense and Education Fund (SALDEF)

items.m: Armed attack on worshippers at a Sikh gurdwara in Oak Creek, Wisconsin; a touchstone for Sikh community safety, hate-crime data and houses-of-worship security advocacy.
Shootings at three metro Atlanta spas killed eight people, most of them Asian women, prompting national attention to anti-Asian violence and gendered hate.
President Biden signed Public Law 117-13, directing expedited federal review of COVID-19-related hate crimes and improved hate-crime reporting.
Executive order establishing the White House Initiative and Advisory Commission on Asian Americans, Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders; it superseded four earlier orders.
Supreme Court ruling on race-conscious admissions at Harvard and UNC; Asian American applicants figured prominently in the case and in community responses.
Wildfire destroyed much of Lahaina on Maui, a historic center of Hawaiian culture; recovery, housing and land questions remain active news stories.
items.o: Wildfire.gov (U.S. interagency wildland fire lessons site)
